## Outline

Under unconfoundedness, ordinary least squares need not estimate the ATE. This
chapter combines outcome regression with inverse propensity weighting to obtain the
augmented inverse propensity weighted (AIPW) score. Cross-fitting then allows us to
use flexible nuisance-function estimates while retaining root-$n$ inference under
appropriate rate and overlap conditions.

## 1. ATE under unconfoundedness

Maintain consistency, i.i.d. sampling,

$$
D_i\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y_i(1),Y_i(0))\mid W_i,
$$

and overlap. Define

$$
\mu_d(w)=\mathbb E[Y_i\mid D_i=d,W_i=w],
\qquad
e(w)=\Pr(D_i=1\mid W_i=w).
$$

Then

$$
\tau=\operatorname{ATE}
=\mathbb E[\mu_1(W_i)-\mu_0(W_i)].
$$

### Why an arbitrary OLS model can fail

In the simulation below, treatment depends on $W$, although it is random
conditional on $W$. The individual effect is $1+W^2$, so the true ATE is 2.
Both displayed regressions omit treatment-related nonlinear functions.

```{webr}
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

set.seed(5280)
n <- 5000
W <- rnorm(n)
V <- rnorm(n)
D <- as.integer(W + V > 0)
epsilon <- rnorm(n)
Y <- 1 + D + W + D * W^2 + sin(W) + epsilon

fit_short <- lm(Y ~ D)
fit_linear <- lm(Y ~ D + W)
rbind(
  short = coeftest(fit_short, vcov. = vcovHC(fit_short, type = "HC2"))["D", ],
  linear = coeftest(fit_linear, vcov. = vcovHC(fit_linear, type = "HC2"))["D", ]
)
```

Identification of the ATE does not make an arbitrary linear working model correct.

## 2. The propensity score and IPW

The propensity score $e(W)$ summarizes how covariates predict treatment.
Rosenbaum and Rubin's balancing-score theorem says that unconfoundedness given $W$
implies

$$
D_i\perp\!\!\!\perp(Y_i(1),Y_i(0))\mid e(W_i).
$$

For $Z_i=(Y_i(1),Y_i(0))$, the key calculation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(D_i=1\mid Z_i,e(W_i))
&=\mathbb E[\mathbb E(D_i\mid Z_i,W_i)\mid Z_i,e(W_i)]\\
&=\mathbb E[e(W_i)\mid Z_i,e(W_i)]\\
&=e(W_i)
=\Pr(D_i=1\mid e(W_i)).
\end{aligned}
$$

The ATE also satisfies

$$
\tau
=\mathbb E\!\left[
\frac{D_iY_i}{e(W_i)}
-\frac{(1-D_i)Y_i}{1-e(W_i)}
\right].
$$

For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{D_iY_i}{e(W_i)}\right]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[
\frac{\mathbb E[D_iY_i(1)\mid W_i]}{e(W_i)}
\right]\\
&=\mathbb E[Y_i(1)].
\end{aligned}
$$

Unconfoundedness factors the conditional expectation in the second step. Overlap is
needed for the denominators, and near-zero denominators explain why IPW can be
unstable even when it is identified.

## 3. AIPW and double robustness

For generic outcome regressions $m_1,m_0$ and propensity function $q$, define

$$
\begin{aligned}
\psi(O_i;m_1,m_0,q)
={}&m_1(W_i)-m_0(W_i)\\
&+\frac{D_i\{Y_i-m_1(W_i)\}}{q(W_i)}
-\frac{(1-D_i)\{Y_i-m_0(W_i)\}}{1-q(W_i)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the true nuisance functions, the oracle AIPW estimator averages these scores.
The score has two useful forms.

### Outcome-regression form

If $m_d=\mu_d$, then

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[
\frac{D_i\{Y_i-\mu_1(W_i)\}}{q(W_i)}\Bigm|W_i
\right]=0
$$

for any admissible $q$, and similarly for controls. The outcome-regression part
therefore identifies the ATE even if the propensity model is wrong.

### IPW form

Algebra also gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\psi(O_i;m_1,m_0,q)
={}&\frac{D_iY_i}{q(W_i)}
-\frac{(1-D_i)Y_i}{1-q(W_i)}\\
&+m_1(W_i)\left\{1-\frac{D_i}{q(W_i)}\right\}
-m_0(W_i)\left\{1-\frac{1-D_i}{1-q(W_i)}\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

If $q=e$, then

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[1-\frac{D_i}{e(W_i)}\Bigm|W_i\right]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E\!\left[1-\frac{1-D_i}{1-e(W_i)}\Bigm|W_i\right]=0.
$$

The conditioning on $W_i$ matters: an unconditional mean-zero equality alone
would not justify multiplying the term by an arbitrary function of $W_i$.

Subject to regularity conditions, the feasible AIPW estimator is consistent if
either both outcome regressions are consistently estimated or the propensity score
is consistently estimated. This is **double robustness**. It does not protect
against failures of unconfoundedness, overlap, consistency, or sampling assumptions.

## 4. Cross-fitting and double machine learning

To prevent own-observation overfitting, partition the sample into folds
$I_1,\ldots,I_K$. For each fold:

1. estimate $\mu_1,\mu_0,e$ using all other folds;
2. evaluate those functions and the AIPW score on the held-out fold;
3. average all held-out scores.

The resulting estimator is

$$
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DML}}
=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{i\in I_k}
\psi\!\left(O_i;
\widehat\mu_1^{(-k)},\widehat\mu_0^{(-k)},\widehat e^{(-k)}
\right).
$$

The AIPW score is orthogonal: small nuisance errors have no first-order effect on
its population expectation. A typical sufficient product-rate condition is

$$
\|\widehat e-e\|_2
\left(\|\widehat\mu_1-\mu_1\|_2+
\|\widehat\mu_0-\mu_0\|_2\right)
=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
$$

If the two relevant mean-squared errors have orders $n^{-a}$ and $n^{-b}$,
their $L^2$ errors have orders $n^{-a/2}$ and $n^{-b/2}$. Exact big-$O$
rates therefore require $a+b>1$; the equality case needs a stronger little-$o$
condition. One should not compare nuisance variances directly without taking square
roots and forming the product remainder.

Under strong overlap, suitable moments, nuisance consistency, and the product-rate
condition,

$$
\sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DML}}-\tau)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N(0,V_{\mathrm{eff}}).
$$

The centered true AIPW score is the efficient influence function for the ATE in the
nonparametric unconfoundedness model. The resulting efficiency statement concerns
regular estimators asymptotically; it does not say AIPW has the smallest variance in
every finite sample.

## 5. Implementation with `grf`

The `grf` implementation uses out-of-bag nuisance predictions to construct an
orthogonalized AIPW estimate. In the model below the true ATE is
$\mathbb E[\max\{W_1,0\}]=1/\sqrt{2\pi}\approx0.399$.

The PDF's substantive code uses $n=2{,}000$ and 4,000 trees. The live cell uses
$n=1{,}000$ and 500 trees for classroom speed. Increase the number of trees and
check stability in final work.

```{webr}
library(grf)

set.seed(5280)
n <- 1000                    # classroom setting; PDF uses 2000
p <- 10
W <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
D <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.4 + 0.2 * (W[, 1] > 0))
Y <- pmax(W[, 1], 0) * D + W[, 2] + pmin(W[, 3], 0) + rnorm(n)

forest_live <- causal_forest(W, Y, D, num.trees = 500)
ate_live <- average_treatment_effect(
  forest_live,
  target.sample = "all",
  method = "AIPW"
)

c(estimate = unname(ate_live["estimate"]),
  std.error = unname(ate_live["std.err"]),
  truth = 1 / sqrt(2 * pi))
```

In applied work, inspect estimated propensities and sensitivity to tuning. Extreme
propensities can produce noisy scores despite double robustness. If overlap is poor,
changing the target population, using a pre-specified trimming rule, or obtaining
better comparison data may be preferable to relying on enormous weights.

## Summary

- The ATE has both outcome-regression and IPW representations under
  unconfoundedness and overlap.
- Arbitrary OLS specifications need not estimate the ATE when treatment depends on
  covariates.
- AIPW is consistent if either the outcome-regression pair or the propensity score
  is consistently estimated, subject to regularity conditions.
- Cross-fitting makes orthogonal scores compatible with flexible nuisance learners.
- Root-$n$ inference requires strong overlap, nuisance consistency, and a product
  of nuisance errors that is $o_p(n^{-1/2})$.
- Statistical robustness cannot repair a failure of the causal identification
  assumptions.
